title: Body Aches After Drinking: Legs, Joints, Muscles and What Helps
excerpt: Why your body, legs, joints, and muscles ache after drinking, what actually helps the morning after, how to use painkillers safely, and the signs that need a doctor.
metaDescription: Why your body aches after drinking: legs, joints, and muscles explained, what helps the morning after, safe painkiller use, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** if your body aches the morning after drinking, it's almost always a normal part of a hangover, not a sign that something is wrong. The aching usually comes from a mix of things that happen at once: your immune system releases inflammatory signals, you lose fluid, you sleep badly, and you probably spent the night standing, dancing, or lying in a strange position. Most of the time it fades within a day. A few patterns are worth taking seriously, though, and this guide covers those too: a hot, swollen joint (often gout), muscle pain with dark urine, and aches that come with shaking and sweating after you stop drinking.

**The quick version of what helps:** drink water with some electrolytes, eat a real meal, rest, and move gently once you can. If you need a painkiller, be careful about which one and how much, because both common options interact with alcohol. And if you get body aches after only a drink or two, or every single time you drink, that's worth mentioning to a doctor.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Get medical help promptly if** a joint (often the big toe, ankle, or knee) becomes suddenly hot, red, swollen, and too painful to touch; your muscles are severely painful or weak and your urine is dark brown or cola-colored; you can't keep fluids down for most of a day; you have a high fever, a stiff neck, or chest pain; or you get tremors, heavy sweating, a racing heart, or confusion within a day or two of stopping after a period of heavy daily drinking, since that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can become dangerous. **Call 911** for chest pain, trouble breathing, a seizure, or severe confusion. Also talk to a doctor if you notice ongoing numbness, tingling, or burning in your feet or hands, or if aches after drinking keep coming back.

## Why Your Body Aches After Drinking

There isn't one single cause. Researchers who study hangovers describe them as a cluster of effects that pile on top of each other, and body aches sit right in the middle of that cluster. Here are the main contributors, roughly from most to least important for a typical night out.

### 1. Inflammation: your immune system's "sick day" signal

When you drink a lot, your body ramps up production of cytokines, the chemical messengers your immune system uses to coordinate a response. Studies measuring blood levels during hangovers have found several of these messengers elevated the next morning, and the degree of change has been linked to how bad people say they feel.

Cytokines are the same signals that make you ache all over when you have the flu. They lower your pain threshold, make you tired, and give you that heavy, "everything hurts" feeling. So when people say a hangover feels like being a bit sick, that's not just a figure of speech. Part of the mechanism really is similar.

Alcohol also irritates the gut lining, which can let more bacterial by-products pass into the blood than usual. That gives the immune system something extra to react to. For a deeper look at this side of alcohol, see our guide to [alcohol and inflammation](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-inflammation-complete-health-impact-guide-2025).

### 2. Dehydration and electrolyte shifts

Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water. The result is that you urinate more than you drink, especially in the first few hours. You also lose sodium, potassium, and magnesium along the way, and if you vomited or sweated a lot while dancing, you lost more.

Mild dehydration on its own can make muscles feel tight, tired, and crampy, and it tends to make headaches worse. It's worth saying that research on hangovers has found dehydration doesn't fully explain how bad people feel. You can rehydrate and still feel rough, because the inflammation and poor sleep are still there. But it's one of the easiest parts to fix, which is why it's first on most lists. Our article on [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers what's worth taking and when.

### 3. Bad sleep lowers your pain threshold

Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but it breaks up sleep in the second half of the night as your body processes it. You get less REM sleep, wake more often, and often wake up too early. That matters for aches because poor sleep makes people more sensitive to pain. Studies of sleep loss have repeatedly found that even one short or broken night makes ordinary discomfort feel worse.

Your muscles also do a lot of their routine repair work while you sleep. A broken night means less of that, which adds to the stiff, unrested feeling.

### 4. What you physically did the night before

This one gets overlooked. A big night often means hours of standing, walking, dancing, or sitting on a hard stool, followed by sleeping in a position you'd never choose sober, sometimes on a couch or floor. Alcohol also dulls pain, so you don't notice the strain in the moment. The next morning you feel all of it at once.

If your aches are mostly in your feet, calves, lower back, or neck, the activity itself is a big part of the story.

### 5. Low blood sugar and depleted energy stores

Processing alcohol keeps your liver busy, which can interfere with its normal job of releasing glucose into your blood. People who drank a lot on an empty stomach can wake with low blood sugar, which can make them feel shaky, weak, and achy. Eating a proper meal with some carbohydrates usually helps quickly.

### 6. Slower muscle recovery

Research on alcohol and exercise has found that heavy drinking after a workout reduces muscle protein synthesis, the process your body uses to repair and rebuild muscle. If you trained hard the day of a night out, or played a sport and then went drinking, expect your normal soreness to linger longer and feel worse. Our article on [alcohol and muscle recovery](/never-hungover/alcohol-protein-synthesis-muscle-recovery-impact-guide-2025) goes into the details.

### 7. Congeners and acetaldehyde

When your liver breaks down alcohol, the first product is acetaldehyde, a toxic compound that contributes to nausea, flushing, and the general feeling of being unwell. Darker drinks such as whiskey, brandy, and red wine also contain more congeners, by-products of fermentation and aging. Some studies have found people report worse hangovers after high-congener drinks than after clear spirits at the same dose. Neither compound specifically targets your muscles, but both feed into the overall "poisoned" feeling that body aches are part of.

## Why Do My Legs Ache After Drinking?

Aching legs are one of the most searched versions of this question, and they have a few likely causes.

- **You were on your feet.** Standing at a bar, walking between venues, or dancing for hours is real exercise for your calves and thighs. Alcohol dulls the signals that would normally tell you to sit down.
- **Fluid and electrolyte loss.** Calf muscles are particularly prone to cramping and tightness when you're low on fluid, sodium, potassium, or magnesium. Night-time leg cramps after drinking are common for this reason.
- **Poor sleep and restless legs.** Some people find alcohol makes restless legs worse, that urge to move your legs at night that disrupts sleep. More movement and less sleep can leave legs feeling heavy and sore.
- **Inflammation.** The same body-wide inflammatory response that causes general aches shows up in big muscle groups like the legs.

For a social drinker, achy legs after a big night almost always fade within a day with fluids, food, and rest. Two patterns are different:

- **Burning, tingling, or numbness in the feet and lower legs that sticks around** is not a hangover symptom. Long-term heavy drinking can damage nerves (a condition called alcoholic neuropathy), and it often starts in the feet. It's worth a doctor visit.
- **One calf that's swollen, warm, red, or painful**, especially after a long flight or a long period of not moving, needs a prompt medical check to rule out a blood clot.

## Why Do My Joints Hurt After Drinking?

Joint pain is different from general muscle aches, and it deserves its own section because the most important cause, gout, is easy to miss.

### Gout: the one to know about

Gout is a form of arthritis caused by uric acid crystals building up in a joint. A gout attack usually comes on suddenly, often at night, and classically hits the big toe, although the ankle, foot, knee, and wrist can be affected too. The joint becomes hot, red, swollen, and so tender that even a bedsheet resting on it hurts.

Alcohol is one of the best-known gout triggers, for two reasons. Your body breaks down purines into uric acid, and beer in particular is high in purines. Alcohol also makes it harder for your kidneys to clear uric acid. Large studies of men followed over many years found that beer was most strongly linked to gout risk, spirits less so, and moderate wine less clearly. A more recent study of people who already had gout found that drinking within the previous day or two raised the risk of a flare, regardless of drink type. A big meal heavy in red meat or seafood alongside the drinks adds to the load.

If you wake up after drinking with one very painful, swollen joint rather than a general all-over ache, think gout and see a doctor, ideally soon. Gout is very treatable, but repeated attacks can damage joints over time, and a hot, swollen joint can occasionally be an infection, which needs urgent care.

### Other reasons joints ache after drinking

- **Inflammatory arthritis flares.** Some people with rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, or other inflammatory conditions notice flares after drinking. The research here is mixed. Some studies even link light drinking with lower rheumatoid arthritis risk. But your own experience matters more than population averages. If drinking reliably sets off your joints, that's useful information to share with your doctor, especially if you take medication such as methotrexate, where alcohol limits are part of the standard advice.
- **Generalized inflammation.** The same cytokine response that causes muscle aches can make joints feel stiff and sore too, usually on both sides of the body and fading within a day.
- **Dehydration.** Joints and the surrounding tissues are sensitive to low fluid levels, and stiffness is common when you're dehydrated.
- **Strain from the night before.** Knees and hips take a beating from dancing, standing, and awkward sleeping positions.

Our article on [alcohol, autoimmune disease, and inflammation](/never-hungover/alcohol-autoimmune-diseases-inflammatory-response-2025) looks at the inflammatory side in more depth.

## Muscle Aches After Drinking: Normal vs. Not Normal

General muscle soreness after a heavy night is very common. Here's how to tell the ordinary version from the kind that needs attention.

| What you notice | Likely meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Dull, all-over aching that fades by evening | Typical hangover: inflammation, dehydration, poor sleep | Fluids, food, rest, gentle movement |
| Sore legs, feet, or back after a long night out | Physical strain from standing, dancing, sleeping awkwardly | Rest, stretching, warm shower |
| Night-time or morning leg cramps | Fluid and electrolyte loss | Water plus electrolytes, gentle stretching |
| One joint suddenly hot, red, swollen, very painful | Possible gout (or, rarely, infection) | See a doctor soon; urgent if you have fever |
| Severe muscle pain or weakness plus dark brown urine | Possible rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown) | Urgent medical care |
| Aches plus shaking, sweating, anxiety, racing heart after stopping heavy daily drinking | Possible alcohol withdrawal | Medical care; don't manage it alone |
| Lasting numbness, tingling, or burning in feet or hands | Possible nerve damage from long-term heavy drinking | Book a doctor visit |
| Aches after only one or two drinks, every time | Could be an intolerance, medication interaction, or underlying condition | Mention it to a doctor |

### A note on rhabdomyolysis

Rhabdomyolysis is a rare but serious condition where damaged muscle tissue breaks down and releases its contents into the blood, which can harm the kidneys. In people who drink, it's most often linked to very heavy binge drinking, lying unconscious or pinned in one position for many hours, extreme exertion while drunk, or combining alcohol with certain drugs. The warning signs are severe muscle pain, weakness, swelling, and dark, tea- or cola-colored urine. That's an emergency. Ordinary hangover aches are nothing like this, but it's worth knowing the signs.

### A note on alcohol withdrawal

For someone who drinks heavily every day, aches that start within a day or so of cutting back can be part of withdrawal, especially when they come with tremors, sweating, nausea, anxiety, a fast heartbeat, or trouble sleeping. Withdrawal can escalate to seizures or a dangerous state of confusion, so it's a medical situation, not something to push through at home. If that sounds like you or someone you know, a doctor can help you stop safely. For most readers of this article, a social drinker with aches after a big weekend, this won't apply.

## What Helps Body Aches After Drinking

There's no cure for a hangover, and nothing will make the aches vanish instantly. These steps have the most sense behind them.

### Rehydrate properly

Sip water steadily rather than chugging a liter at once, which can make nausea worse. Adding electrolytes helps you hold onto the fluid. An oral rehydration drink, a sports drink, broth, or coconut water all work. If your urine is pale yellow by midday, you're on track.

### Eat a real meal

Eggs, toast, oatmeal, bananas, rice, soup, or whatever you can manage. Food brings your blood sugar back up, replaces some of the salt and potassium you lost, and gives your body the raw materials to recover. Bananas and potatoes are good sources of potassium. Leafy greens, nuts, and whole grains provide magnesium.

### Move gently, once you can

It sounds wrong, but light movement often helps aches more than lying still. A short walk, some easy stretching, or a few minutes of yoga gets blood moving through stiff muscles. Skip hard workouts until you've rehydrated and eaten. Exercising hard while dehydrated and hungover raises the risk of cramps and, in rare extreme cases, muscle injury.

### Warm shower or bath

Heat relaxes tight muscles and many people find it eases general aches. Don't go straight into a very hot bath or sauna if you're still lightheaded or dehydrated, as heat can make dizziness worse.

### Sleep it off if you can

Since poor sleep makes pain worse, a nap or an early night is one of the most effective "treatments" there is. It's not exciting advice, but it works.

## Can You Take a Painkiller for Body Aches After Drinking?

Often yes, with care. But this is where people most often make mistakes, because both of the common choices clash with alcohol in different ways.

- **Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin (NSAIDs)** are good at easing muscle and joint aches because they work on inflammation. The trade-off is your stomach and kidneys. Alcohol already irritates the stomach lining, and NSAIDs add to that, raising the risk of irritation and bleeding. Their labels carry a warning for people who have 3 or more drinks a day. They can also strain the kidneys when you're dehydrated, which after a night of drinking you probably are. If you use one, rehydrate first, take it with food, and stick to the label dose. Read more in our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol).
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** is easier on the stomach but processed by the liver, and the label warns about severe liver damage in people who have 3 or more drinks every day. A single standard dose after the alcohol has cleared is unlikely to harm a healthy adult who doesn't drink heavily day to day, but don't stack doses, and check other products for hidden acetaminophen. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the details.
- **Don't take painkillers "just in case" before bed** while alcohol is still in your system. Wait until morning, see whether you actually need one, and take it after eating.
- **If you suspect gout,** don't just self-treat with painkillers and hope. Gout has specific treatments, and some common choices are worse than others. Aspirin, for example, can affect uric acid levels. See a doctor.

> **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist** before using any painkiller after drinking if you have stomach ulcers, kidney or liver disease, heart disease, or high blood pressure, take blood thinners or other regular medicines, or drink 3 or more drinks most days.

## How to Prevent Body Aches the Next Time

Prevention comes down to reducing the factors listed above. None of these is magic, but together they make a real difference.

1. **Drink less, and drink slower.** This is the only step with strong evidence. The amount you drink is the biggest predictor of how bad the next day feels.
2. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows the rate alcohol reaches your blood and helps keep blood sugar steadier.
3. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water between drinks keeps you more hydrated and naturally slows your pace.
4. **Go easier on dark drinks.** Clear spirits tend to produce milder hangovers than high-congener drinks at the same dose, at least in some studies.
5. **If you're prone to gout, go easy on beer especially,** and avoid pairing a big night of drinking with a large red-meat or seafood meal. Ask your doctor about your personal triggers.
6. **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed if you can, and give yourself a chance to sleep in.
7. **Don't drink to numb an injury or after a hard workout** if you can avoid it. Alcohol hides the pain and slows recovery.
8. **Take care of your body during the night.** Sit down sometimes, wear comfortable shoes, and get home to an actual bed.

Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers these and a few more in more detail.

## Where Does DHM Fit In?

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's sold as a hangover supplement. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, which suggest it may support alcohol metabolism and reduce some of the oxidative stress and inflammation drinking causes. Human data is limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents body aches specifically, and it won't undo the effects of drinking too much, dehydration, or a night of dancing.

If you want to try DHM as part of a sensible routine, rather than as a replacement for drinking less, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when. If you take regular medication, check with a pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Body aches after drinking are common and usually come from inflammation, dehydration, poor sleep, and physical strain from the night before. They normally fade within a day.
- Aching legs are usually about standing, dancing, and fluid loss. Lasting numbness or burning in your feet is different and worth a doctor visit.
- A single hot, red, swollen, very painful joint after drinking may be gout. See a doctor rather than waiting it out.
- Severe muscle pain with dark urine, or aches with shaking and sweating after stopping heavy daily drinking, need medical care.
- Water with electrolytes, a real meal, gentle movement, and sleep help most. If you use a painkiller, choose carefully and stick to the label.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my whole body ache after drinking alcohol?**

Usually because several things happen at once. Heavy drinking triggers an inflammatory response similar to a mild illness, alcohol makes you lose fluid and electrolytes, it breaks up your sleep (which makes you more sensitive to pain), and a night out often involves hours of standing, dancing, or sleeping in an awkward position. Together these produce the all-over ache most people feel the next morning. It normally fades within a day.

**Why do my legs ache after drinking?**

Most often it's a mix of being on your feet for hours, losing fluid and electrolytes such as sodium, potassium, and magnesium, and poor sleep. Calf muscles are especially prone to tightness and cramps when you're dehydrated. Water with electrolytes, food, rest, and gentle stretching usually help. If you have lasting numbness, tingling, or burning in your feet, or one calf is swollen, warm, and painful, see a doctor.

**Why do my joints hurt after drinking alcohol?**

General stiffness can come from inflammation, dehydration, and physical strain. But if a single joint, often the big toe, ankle, or knee, suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen, and very painful, that's a classic sign of gout, which alcohol (especially beer) is well known to trigger. Some people with inflammatory arthritis also notice flares after drinking. A hot, swollen joint should be checked by a doctor.

**How long do body aches last after drinking?**

For most people, hangover aches ease within 24 hours, often by the evening of the next day once they've rehydrated, eaten, and rested. Aches that last several days, keep getting worse, or come with fever, dark urine, severe weakness, or a swollen joint are not typical hangover symptoms and should be checked by a doctor.

**What is the best thing to take for body aches after drinking?**

Start with water plus electrolytes, a proper meal, rest, and gentle movement. If you need a painkiller, ibuprofen or naproxen help with aches but are harder on the stomach and kidneys, so take them with food and water after rehydrating. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is easier on the stomach but processed by the liver, so take only a single standard dose after the alcohol has cleared. Ask a pharmacist first if you have health conditions, take other medicines, or drink 3 or more drinks most days.

**Can body aches after drinking be a sign of alcohol withdrawal?**

They can in people who drink heavily every day. Withdrawal aches usually start within a day or so of cutting back and come with tremors, sweating, nausea, anxiety, a racing heart, or trouble sleeping. Withdrawal can become dangerous, so it needs medical care rather than toughing it out. For a social drinker with aches after a big night, the cause is almost always an ordinary hangover.

**When are muscle aches after drinking an emergency?**

Get urgent care if you have severe muscle pain, weakness, or swelling together with dark brown or cola-colored urine, which can signal rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown that can harm the kidneys). Also seek help for chest pain, trouble breathing, a seizure, severe confusion, or a high fever with a stiff neck. Call 911 in an emergency.

**Does DHM help with body aches after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or relieves body aches specifically. Animal and lab research suggests it may support alcohol metabolism and reduce some inflammation and oxidative stress, but human data is limited. The most reliable ways to avoid next-day aches are drinking less and more slowly, eating, staying hydrated, and getting decent sleep.
